The last 15 questions are three passage sets (factual, narrative, literary) of 5 questions each; each set stays together.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to RECTIFY:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Correct
Why: Rectify means to put right a mistake or a fault.
Why not the others: (A) only looks similar. (B) and (D) have different meanings.
Key point: Please rectify the errors in your form.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After the long war, both countries signed a ________ treaty.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) peace
Why: "Peace" means freedom from war; a peace treaty ends a war.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) mean a part or parts of something. (D) is an adjective and would give "a peaceful treaty", which changes the meaning.
Key point: A piece of cake; peace after war.

questions.sub_topic: The medicine that the doctor prescribed
questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. The medicine
B. must be taken twice a day
C. that the doctor prescribed
D. after meals
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, C, B, D
Why: "The medicine (A) that the doctor prescribed (C) must be taken twice a day (B) after meals (D)." The "that" clause must follow "The medicine".
Why not the others: (B) moves the "that" clause away from "The medicine", so it seems to describe the day. (C) and (D) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: A relative clause sits right after the noun it describes.

questions.sub_topic: Figures: transferred epithet, apostrophe, onomatopoeia, paradox
questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Transferred epithet
(B) Apostrophe
(C) Onomatopoeia
(D) Paradox

List-II
(I) The rain went pitter-patter on the leaves.
(II) Child is the father of the man.
(III) O river, carry my boat safely home!
(IV) She sat through the anxious hours of the operation.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The hours are not anxious; she is — transferred epithet (IV); speaking to the river — apostrophe (III); "pitter-patter" imitates sound — onomatopoeia (I); a child being the father of the man seems absurd but holds a truth — paradox (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps transferred epithet and apostrophe; (C) swaps apostrophe and onomatopoeia; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: A paradox seems self-contradictory but reveals a truth.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The two brothers had a long ________ about who would sit by the window.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) argument
Why: After "a long", a noun is needed: "a long argument". (Note that "argue" drops its "e": argument.)
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) is a verb form. (D) is an adjective.
Key point: Argue drops the "e" in argument.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
After the flood, the village was DESOLATE, with not a single family left.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Deserted
Why: Desolate means empty of people and bleak; deserted means the same.
Why not the others: (B) is the opposite. (C) is unrelated. (D) misses the sense of emptiness and gloom.
Key point: The sentence ("not a single family left") explains the word.

questions.question:
Select the words that mean "lively and full of energy":
A. vivacious
B. vicious
C. sprightly
D. spiteful
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
C) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A and C only
Why: "Vivacious" and "sprightly" both mean lively and full of energy.
Why not the others: B (vicious) means cruel or violent. D (spiteful) means wanting to hurt or annoy. Options (A), (B) and (C) include one of them.
Key point: Vivacious and vicious look alike but are almost opposites in feeling.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ we reached the station, the train had already left.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) By the time
Why: "By the time" means "not later than the moment when"; the train had left before we arrived (past perfect).
Why not the others: (A) suggests the train left just as we arrived, which clashes with "had already". (B) and (C) show condition.
Key point: By the time + past simple, past perfect in the main clause.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. a long line
B. During the fire drill, the students
C. on the playground
D. formed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, A, C
Why: The opener with the subject (B) is followed by the verb (D), the object (A) and the place (C).
Why not the others: (A) puts the object before the verb. (C) and (D) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: Subject, verb, object, then place.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. so beautiful
B. seen a sunset
C. Rarely have I
D. as the one at Kanyakumari
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C, B, A, D
Why: "Rarely have I (C) seen a sunset (B) so beautiful (A) as the one at Kanyakumari (D)." "Have I" is completed by "seen", and "so ... as" makes the comparison.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) start with a lower-case part. (B) separates "have I" from "seen".
Key point: Rarely + auxiliary + subject + past participle.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The path was steep and slippery; ________, the old man reached the temple at the top.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) nevertheless
Why: "Nevertheless" means "in spite of that"; he reached the top despite the difficult path.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) show a result, which is illogical. (B) adds a point.
Key point: Nevertheless = however, despite this.

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: ancient, sorrow, shallow, dawn
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. ancient — modern
B. sorrow — grief
C. shallow — deep
D. dawn — dusk
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, C and D only
C) B, C and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, C and D only
Why: Ancient and modern, shallow and deep, dawn and dusk are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair B is a pair of synonyms — sorrow means grief. Options (B), (C) and (D) include pair B.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
All students must ________ their project reports by Monday.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) hand in
Why: "Hand in" means to submit work to a teacher or an authority.
Why not the others: (B) means to distribute. (C) means to pass on to a younger generation. (D) needs a person after it ("hand over to the teacher").
Key point: Students hand in work; teachers hand out papers.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
I will ________ come to your birthday party.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) definitely
Why: The correct spelling is d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e-l-y, from "definite".
Why not the others: (A) has "a" in place of "i". (B) misses the "e". (C) has "e" in place of the first "i".
Key point: Definitely contains "finite".

questions.sub_topic: Idioms in sentences: nick of time, feather in one's cap, drop of a hat, on the house
questions.question:
Match the sentences in List-I with the idioms in List-II that best complete them:

List-I
(A) The ambulance arrived ____, just as his breathing grew weak.
(B) Winning the national award was ____ for the young scientist.
(C) She is so helpful that she will lend you money ____.
(D) The owner was so pleased that he said our dinner was ____.

List-II
(I) in the nick of time
(II) a feather in her cap
(III) at the drop of a hat
(IV) on the house
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: In the nick of time — just in time (I); a feather in one's cap — an achievement to be proud of (II); at the drop of a hat — immediately, without hesitating (III); on the house — free, paid for by the owner (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Fit the idiom to the whole situation in the sentence.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: the number, a number, best of two, subjects
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. The number of students has increased this year.
B. A number of students was absent today.
C. He is the best of the two brothers.
D. Mathematics and physics are my favourite subjects.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A and D only
Why: In A, "the number" is singular ("has"). In D, two subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb.
Why not the others: B should be "were" ("a number of" means many). C should be "the better of the two" (the comparative is used for two). Options (A), (B) and (D) include B or C.
Key point: The number of ... is; a number of ... are.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Please ________ that all the windows are shut before you leave the laboratory.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ensure
Why: "Ensure" means to make certain that something happens.
Why not the others: (A) "Insure" means to protect against loss with an insurance policy. (C) "Assure" means to tell someone confidently to remove doubt, and needs a person as object ("assure me that"). (D) is an adjective.
Key point: Ensure a result; insure a car; assure a person.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
Ravi is always PUNCTUAL for his classes.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Late
Why: Punctual means arriving at the right time; late means arriving after it.
Why not the others: (A) is close to punctual. (B) and (D) are other good habits, not opposites.
Key point: A punctual train arrives on time.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Illegible
(B) Invincible
(C) Inaudible
(D) Inaccessible

List-II
(I) That cannot be heard
(II) That cannot be reached
(III) That cannot be read
(IV) That cannot be defeated
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Illegible — cannot be read (III); invincible — cannot be defeated (IV); inaudible — cannot be heard (I); inaccessible — cannot be reached (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps illegible and invincible; (B) swaps invincible and inaudible; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Leg-" read, "vinc-" conquer, "aud-" hear, "access" reach.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Mumbai was ________ known as Bombay.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) formerly
Why: "Formerly" means in the past, earlier.
Why not the others: (B) means in an official or proper way. (C) is a misspelling. (D) is a noun.
Key point: Formerly = before; formally = officially.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
A single bite of this snake can be ________ to a human being if not treated quickly.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) lethal
Why: "Lethal" means able to cause death.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) contradict "if not treated quickly". (D) does not fit "can be ... to a human being".
Key point: "If not treated quickly" signals serious danger.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The nation ________ tribute to the soldiers who died defending the border.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) paid
Why: The fixed collocation is "pay tribute to".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not go with "tribute".
Key point: Pay tribute, pay attention, pay a compliment.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The villagers are strongly opposed ________ the cutting of the forest.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) to
Why: The expression is "opposed to" something.
Why not the others: (A) "Against" follows "oppose" in some informal use but not "opposed". (C) and (D) are wrong.
Key point: Opposed to, objection to.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
He said, "I am busy today."
options: A) He said that he was busy that day.
B) He said that I am busy today.
C) He said that he is busy that day.
D) He told that he was busy today.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) He said that he was busy that day.
Why: With a past reporting verb, "am" becomes "was", "I" becomes "he" and "today" becomes "that day".
Why not the others: (B) keeps the pronoun and tense. (C) keeps the present tense. (D) uses "told" without an object and keeps "today".
Key point: Change tense, pronoun and time word together.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The minister said that the new hospital"
A. by the end of next year
B. and would have
C. would be ready
D. five hundred beds
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C, A, B, D
Why: "... the new hospital would be ready (C) by the end of next year (A) and would have (B) five hundred beds (D)." Each "would" verb is followed by what completes it.
Why not the others: (A) begins with "and". (B) gives "would be ready five hundred beds". (C) begins with "five hundred beds", which has no verb.
Key point: Join two verbs with "and" after the first is complete.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Make up
(B) Make out
(C) Make up for
(D) Make off with

List-II
(I) Compensate for
(II) Steal and run away with
(III) Invent a story, or become friends again after a quarrel
(IV) Manage to see, hear or understand
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Make up an excuse, or make up after a quarrel (III); make out a faint sign — manage to see it (IV); make up for lost time — compensate (I); thieves make off with jewels — steal them (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps make up and make out; (B) swaps make out and make up for; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Adding a preposition ("for", "with") changes the meaning again.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
A ________ writer, she has published more than sixty novels.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) prolific
Why: "Prolific" means producing a great deal of work.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not explain sixty novels.
Key point: The number of novels explains the word.

questions.sub_topic: A list of topics for a meeting
questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A list of items to be discussed at a meeting"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Agenda
Why: An agenda lists what will be discussed at a meeting.
Why not the others: (A) is the written record of what was said after the meeting. (B) is a written note or message. (D) is a list of goods or books.
Key point: The agenda comes before the meeting; the minutes after.

questions.sub_topic: How a seed becomes a plant
questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. Soon afterwards, a tiny shoot pushes upwards towards the light.
B. When a seed gets enough water and warmth, it begins to swell.
C. Its seed coat then splits, and a small root grows down into the soil.
D. Once its first leaves open, the young plant can make its own food.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, C, A, D
Why: B begins with the seed swelling; C follows ("Its seed coat then splits", a root grows down); A follows ("Soon afterwards, a tiny shoot"); D ends with the first leaves.
Why not the others: (A) sends up the shoot before the coat splits. (C) begins with "Its", which has nothing to refer to. (D) opens the leaves before the shoot appears.
Key point: Time words ("then", "soon afterwards", "once") show the order.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
Who wrote this book?
options: A) Who was this book written?
B) By whom was this book written?
C) By whom this book was written?
D) Whom was this book written by him?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) By whom was this book written?
Why: "Who" as the subject becomes "By whom" in the passive, followed by the question order "was this book written?"
Why not the others: (A) drops "by". (C) uses statement order in a question. (D) adds an extra "him".
Key point: Who → By whom.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The lift has stopped working because of poor ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) maintenance
Why: After "poor", a noun is needed: "poor maintenance". Note the spelling: maintain, but maintenance.
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) and (C) are verb forms.
Key point: Maintain changes its spelling to form "maintenance".

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to VIRTUE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Vice
Why: A virtue is a good moral quality; a vice is a bad one.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (C) and (D) are unrelated.
Key point: Patience is a virtue; greed is a vice.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to OBSEQUIOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Servile
Why: Obsequious means too eager to please or obey; servile means the same.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) only look similar.
Key point: An obsequious clerk bows and flatters his manager.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: needle in a haystack, jump the gun, skin of one's teeth, tip of the iceberg
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A needle in a haystack
(B) To jump the gun
(C) By the skin of one's teeth
(D) The tip of the iceberg

List-II
(I) Something almost impossible to find
(II) To act too soon, before the right time
(III) Only just; very narrowly
(IV) A small, visible part of a much larger problem
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: A needle in a haystack — almost impossible to find (I); jump the gun — act too early (II); by the skin of one's teeth — only just (III); the tip of the iceberg — a small part of a big problem (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The class monitor is responsible ________ keeping the attendance register.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) for
Why: One is "responsible for" a task or a result. ("Responsible to" means answerable to a person.)
Why not the others: (B) and (D) are wrong. (C) would mean "answerable to keeping", which makes no sense.
Key point: Responsible for a duty; responsible to a person.

questions.sub_topic: What coral polyps are related to
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A coral reef looks like a garden of brightly coloured rocks, but it is built by animals. Each coral is made up of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps, relatives of jellyfish, which build hard skeletons of limestone around themselves. Over hundreds of years these skeletons pile up into reefs large enough to be seen from space.

Most reef-building corals cannot survive alone. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae that use sunlight to make food, and they share much of this food with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae shelter. The algae also give corals their colours.

This partnership is delicate. When the sea becomes too warm for several weeks, the stressed corals push the algae out of their bodies. Without them, the corals lose both their colour and most of their food, and only the white skeleton shows through the clear tissue. This is called coral bleaching. If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the coral may recover; if the heat lasts, the coral starves and dies.

Reefs cover far less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all known sea species. They protect coasts by breaking the force of waves, and millions of people depend on them for fish and tourism. In India, reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

As the oceans warm, bleaching has become more frequent and more widespread. Scientists say that cutting the gases that heat the planet, together with reducing pollution and overfishing, offers reefs their best chance of survival.

Question: According to the passage, coral polyps are relatives of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Jellyfish
Why: "Each coral is made up of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps, relatives of jellyfish."
Why not the others: (A) and (D) describe what reefs look like or are made of, not what polyps are. (B) The algae live inside corals; they are not relatives.
Key point: Corals are animals, though reefs look like rocks or gardens.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In India, reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

As the oceans warm, bleaching has become more frequent and more widespread. Scientists say that cutting the gases that heat the planet, together with reducing pollution and overfishing, offers reefs their best chance of survival.

Question: Why do bleached corals turn white?
options: A) They have expelled their algae, so the white skeleton shows
B) Salt in the water has slowly painted their skeletons white
C) The hot sun has burnt away all of the polyps on the reef
D) Cold water has frozen over the whole surface of the reef
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) They have expelled their algae, so the white skeleton shows
Why: The stressed corals push the algae out; without them, "the corals lose both their colour ... and only the white skeleton shows through the clear tissue."
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not stated. (D) Bleaching is caused by warm, not cold, water.
Key point: Link the effect (white colour) to its stated cause.

questions.sub_topic: Meaning of the partnership is delicate
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A coral reef looks like a garden of brightly coloured rocks, but it is built by animals. Each coral is made up of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps, relatives of jellyfish, which build hard skeletons of limestone around themselves. Over hundreds of years these skeletons pile up into reefs large enough to be seen from space.

Most reef-building corals cannot survive alone. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae that use sunlight to make food, and they share much of this food with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae shelter. The algae also give corals their colours.

This partnership is delicate. When the sea becomes too warm for several weeks, the stressed corals push the algae out of their bodies. Without them, the corals lose both their colour and most of their food, and only the white skeleton shows through the clear tissue. This is called coral bleaching. If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the coral may recover; if the heat lasts, the coral starves and dies.

Reefs cover far less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all known sea species. They protect coasts by breaking the force of waves, and millions of people depend on them for fish and tourism. In India, reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

As the oceans warm, bleaching has become more frequent and more widespread. Scientists say that cutting the gases that heat the planet, together with reducing pollution and overfishing, offers reefs their best chance of survival.

Question: "This partnership is delicate." The writer means that the relationship between corals and algae:
options: A) Is beautiful to look at under water
B) Exists only in very deep parts of the sea
C) Is harmful to both the coral and the algae
D) Can be easily broken by changes in conditions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Can be easily broken by changes in conditions
Why: The next sentences show how a few weeks of warm water make corals expel the algae.
Why not the others: (A) confuses "delicate" with "pretty". (B) is not stated. (C) The passage shows that both benefit.
Key point: The sentences after a claim usually support it.

They protect coasts by breaking the force of waves, and millions of people depend on them for fish and tourism. In India, reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

As the oceans warm, bleaching has become more frequent and more widespread. Scientists say that cutting the gases that heat the planet, together with reducing pollution and overfishing, offers reefs their best chance of survival.

Question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: A) A bleached coral is always already dead
B) A bleached coral can survive if the water cools in time
C) Bleaching happens only in the Gulf of Mannar
D) Algae can live on their own without any shelter
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A bleached coral can survive if the water cools in time
Why: The passage says, "If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the coral may recover." So bleaching is not always death.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts this. (C) Indian reefs are listed, but bleaching is described as widespread. (D) is not stated.
Key point: Avoid options with "always" or "only" unless the passage says so.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A coral reef looks like a garden of brightly coloured rocks, but it is built by animals. Each coral is made up of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps, relatives of jellyfish, which build hard skeletons of limestone around themselves. Over hundreds of years these skeletons pile up into reefs large enough to be seen from space.

Most reef-building corals cannot survive alone. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae that use sunlight to make food, and they share much of this food with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae shelter. The algae also give corals their colours.

This partnership is delicate. When the sea becomes too warm for several weeks, the stressed corals push the algae out of their bodies. Without them, the corals lose both their colour and most of their food, and only the white skeleton shows through the clear tissue. This is called coral bleaching. If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the coral may recover; if the heat lasts, the coral starves and dies.

Reefs cover far less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all known sea species. They protect coasts by breaking the force of waves, and millions of people depend on them for fish and tourism. In India, reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

As the oceans warm, bleaching has become more frequent and more widespread. Scientists say that cutting the gases that heat the planet, together with reducing pollution and overfishing, offers reefs their best chance of survival.

Question: According to the passage, why are coral reefs important even though they cover a small area?
options: A) They provide most of the world's limestone
B) They are the largest structures built by human beings
C) They supply the algae that people eat as food
D) They support many sea species and protect coasts and livelihoods
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) They support many sea species and protect coasts and livelihoods
Why: Reefs are "home to roughly a quarter of all known sea species", "protect coasts by breaking the force of waves", and support fishing and tourism.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not stated. (B) Reefs are built by animals, not people.
Key point: "Yet" introduces the contrast between small size and great value.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Sister Leela's night shift at the district hospital began at eight, when the visitors were sent home and the long corridor grew quiet. There were twenty-six patients in the general ward and one other nurse, a nervous girl in her first month, who kept asking whether she was doing things right.

At half past eleven, a farmer carried in his small son, wrapped in a blanket and burning with fever. The boy's lips were dry, and he did not open his eyes when Leela spoke to him. The doctor on duty was in the operation theatre. Leela sponged the child with cool water, checked his temperature every fifteen minutes and sent the young nurse running for the doctor the moment the reading rose again.

At two o'clock, the power failed. For a terrible minute the ward was black and silent; then the generator coughed, choked and started, and the lights flickered back. Leela, who had been standing by the boy's bed with a torch in her teeth and the drip in her hand, let out a breath she had not known she was holding.

By morning the fever had broken. The boy opened his eyes, looked around at the strange room and asked for his mother. The farmer, who had not slept, tried to give Leela a hundred-rupee note. She shook her head and pointed to the young nurse. "Thank her," she said. "She ran faster than anyone."

At eight, Leela handed over the ward, caught the bus home and fell asleep with her shoes on. Nobody would ever write about her night. She did not expect anyone to.

Question: Who was on duty with Sister Leela in the general ward?
options: B) A new and nervous nurse
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A new and nervous nurse
Why: "There were twenty-six patients in the general ward and one other nurse, a nervous girl in her first month."
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not stated. (D) The doctor was in the operation theatre.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line.

Question: Leela "let out a breath she had not known she was holding". This shows that she:

B) Was having difficulty breathing in the dark
C) Was angry that the generator was slow
D) Had fallen asleep for a moment
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Had been very tense without realising it
Why: Holding one's breath unconsciously is a sign of fear and tension; when the lights returned, the tension was released.
Why not the others: (B) takes the phrase literally. (C) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: Physical details reveal hidden feelings.

D) She was angry that the young nurse had been slow

Question: "Nobody would ever write about her night. She did not expect anyone to." What do these lines suggest about Leela?
options: A) She was disappointed that no newspaper reported her work
B) She wished to become famous for saving the boy
C) She found her work dull and wanted another job
D) She did her demanding work without seeking recognition
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) She did her demanding work without seeking recognition
Why: After a night of saving a child, she simply goes home and sleeps; she neither gets nor wants praise.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) contradict "She did not expect anyone to." (C) is not suggested.
Key point: Endings often state the character's central quality quietly.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In Praise of an Old Bicycle

It has no gears, no shining paint,
its bell is hoarse, its saddle torn;
it was my grandfather's, then my father's,
and it was rattling before I was born.

It squeaks on every second turn
like an old man who hums off-key;
it does not hurry, does not boast,
and it has never once failed me.

It took my father to his first job,
my mother to her wedding day,
sat patient outside the hospital
the morning I was on my way.

Now it carries me to school,
past honking cars that sweat and fume,
stuck in their own impatient smoke —
while my old bicycle finds room.

I know a new one would be faster;
my friends all laugh and say I should.
But who would sell a friend for speed?
Not I. Not while its wheels are good.

Question: "It squeaks on every second turn / like an old man who hums off-key." The figure of speech used here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Simile
Why: The squeak is compared to an old man's humming using "like" — a simile.
Why not the others: (A) needs no "like" or "as". (C) No opposite words are joined. (D) There is no exaggeration.
Key point: "Like" or "as" marks a simile.

Question: What does the third stanza tell us about the bicycle?
options: A) It was bought new for the speaker's birthday
B) It was often broken and needed repairs
C) It has been part of important moments in the family's life
D) It was used only for carrying goods to market
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It has been part of important moments in the family's life
Why: It took the father to his first job, the mother to her wedding, and waited outside the hospital on the morning the speaker was born.
Why not the others: (A) It belonged to the grandfather first. (B) It "has never once failed me". (D) is not stated.
Key point: Summarise the details of a stanza.

Question: "Past honking cars that sweat and fume, / stuck in their own impatient smoke." What contrast does the poet draw?
options: A) Proud, hurried cars are stuck, while the humble old bicycle moves on
B) Cars are faster than bicycles in every kind of traffic
C) The bicycle produces more smoke than the cars do
D) Cars are kinder to the speaker than his friends are
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Proud, hurried cars are stuck, while the humble old bicycle moves on
Why: The cars are personified as sweating, fuming and impatient, yet stuck; the old bicycle "finds room" and keeps going.
Why not the others: (B) is the opposite of what the stanza shows. (C) Bicycles make no smoke. (D) is not suggested.
Key point: Personification can be used to make fun of the thing personified.

Question: "But who would sell a friend for speed?" The bicycle is called a "friend" because the speaker:
options: A) Received it from a friend at school
B) Wants to sell it to one of his friends
C) Thinks a new bicycle would be friendlier
D) Feels loyalty and affection for it
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Feels loyalty and affection for it
Why: The poem has shown the bicycle's faithful service to three generations; the speaker refuses to replace it out of loyalty.
Why not the others: (A) It came from his grandfather. (B) is the opposite. (C) is not suggested.
Key point: A rhetorical question expects an obvious answer, here "no one".
